weeks.title: Make technology work for you
weeks.summary: Set up a comfortable workspace, organize a calendar, and solve everyday device problems.
objectives: Adjust device and browser settings for a task, then restore them.
Create a practice appointment and choose what others can see.
Pick the right connection and printer, and preview before printing.
Check what an automatic feature changed before you accept it.
Ask for help clearly and give useful feedback.
agenda: Warm-up and goals

Logins; show text size and lesson navigation. Warm-up: hold up an HDMI, a USB and an Ethernet cable and ask what each one did in Level 1. Pairs share slide 2 (one task they do well, one to make easier); learners write worksheet task 1. Read the goals on slide 1 aloud.
Pre-test

Slide 3. Learners type their name first, then work quietly; read directions aloud without suggesting answers. Record each score out of 20 on your roster; print page 1 only if a paper copy is needed. Early finishers read slide 4; late finishers may run to minute 38.
Introduction: the routine
Tell: slide 4, Choose, Test, Restore. Play chapter 1. This routine is the Review language for every cycle.
Cycle A: reading comfort

Tell: slide 5. Show: chapter 2, then zoom live in Edge with Ctrl and +; pause chapter 2 at 1:24. Do: slide 6 and worksheet task 2, every learner at their own seat. Review: a partner confirms the page is back to 100%. Then Tell and Show only: chapter 3 (pause at 2:02 for the prediction) and Settings › System › Display › Scale on the projector.
Cycle B: hearing and screen

Tell: slide 7. Show: chapter 4, then choose the sound output live from the speaker icon on the taskbar. Do: worksheet task 3 with a headset, every learner. Review: the slide 20 knowledge check. Point to the monitor brightness buttons; do not change them.
Cycle C: connections and printing

Tell: slides 11 and 12 (laser for lots of text, inkjet for color and photos). Show: chapter 6, then Ctrl and P live on page 1 of the worksheet (printer name, Pages 1, Copies 1). Do: worksheet tasks 7 and 4, every learner; do not print. Review: a partner reads back the printer and pages; ask aloud which printer suits 200 flyers. Optional: slide 9 and chapter 5, which Level 1 covered.
Cycle D: calendar

Tell: slides 13 and 15. Show: chapter 7. Do: worksheet task 5 on the paper form, marked simulated, unless a demonstration account is set up; switch views on slide 15. Then Tell and Show: slide 14 and chapter 8 (pause at 5:36). Do: worksheet task 6, every learner. Review: the slide 21 knowledge check; a partner checks the five fields.
Cycle E: automation and help

Tell: slides 16 and 19 (slide 17 in one sentence). Show: chapter 9, then in Word type teh and a space and undo with Ctrl and Z. Do: worksheet task 8, every learner. Review: a partner gives one specific piece of feedback.
Individual check

Play chapter 10 (pause at 6:28). Each learner shows you three things: zoom and reset, choose the headset and test it, and preview page 1 on the right printer. Mark Independent, With prompt or Needs practice on the roster; re-model only the missing step.
Apply and close

Slides 23 and 24. Home task: on your own device, make one change from today, write down how you undid it, and share it at the start of week 2. Restore lab settings, then select Start fresh on this computer.

slides.title: Your starting point
slides.body: Name a digital task you already do well. Choose one task you want to make easier.

slides.title: Take the pre-test
slides.body: This is a starting snapshot. Type your name first, answer on your own, then let your instructor record your score.

slides.title: Change one setting; check the result
slides.body: Decide what you need. Make one adjustment. Try the task again. Keep or undo the change.

slides.title: Make text comfortable
slides.body: Browser zoom changes a webpage, and the browser remembers it for each site. Display scaling changes the whole desktop. Start with the control that matches your problem.

slides.title: Practice: zoom without losing your place
slides.body: Use Ctrl and + to enlarge a page; Ctrl and - to reduce it; Ctrl and 0 to reset. On a Mac, use Command. Try this page’s text-size buttons too.

slides.title: Sound and screen checks
slides.body: Choose the correct speaker or headset before adjusting volume. Brightness changes light output; contrast changes separation between light and dark. On a desktop computer, brightness is set with the buttons on the monitor.

slides.title: Browser choices belong to you
slides.body: Review the home page, downloads location and site permissions in Settings. A helpful default should fit your task. Restore shared-lab settings before leaving.

slides.title: Processing, storage, and connections
slides.body: The processor carries out instructions. Memory holds current work. Storage keeps files. A matching connector shape alone does not guarantee every feature.

slides.title: Match a connection to its job
slides.body: Select each card to reveal a useful connection. Read the device label before buying or plugging in a cable.
cards: An external display
HDMI commonly carries video and sound. USB-C video support depends on the device and cable.
A wired network
Ethernet connects a device to a network.
A keyboard or flash drive
USB carries data and power. USB-C can also charge a laptop and, on some devices, connect a display.

slides.title: Printer choices
slides.body: Laser printers use toner and cost less per page for lots of text. Inkjet printers use liquid ink and suit color and photos. Windows and your browser may pick the last printer you used, so check the printer name every time.

slides.title: Print one page before twenty
slides.body: Check the printer name and connection. Open print preview. Select one page, orientation and copies. When printing is allowed, send one test page and check it.

slides.title: A calendar entry needs enough detail
slides.body: Create a fictional library visit: title, day, start and end, location and reminder. Check the time zone when an event involves another region.

slides.title: Share availability thoughtfully
slides.body: Free/busy can show when you are unavailable without the event’s private details. Verify the actual sharing options before inviting someone.

slides.title: Switch the calendar view
slides.body: Use day view for detail, week view for conflicts and month view for the larger picture. A task can have a due date without reserving meeting time.

slides.title: Automation still needs a check
slides.body: A mail rule can sort or flag messages automatically. Autocorrect changes likely mistakes; autocomplete suggests the rest. Review names, addresses and meaning before accepting.

slides.title: Cloud services use another computer
slides.body: Online storage and web apps use a provider’s computers over a network. Check account, connection and save status when you switch devices.

slides.title: Watch: choose settings and verify
slides.body: Follow the worked examples, pause for practice, and choose a chapter to replay a skill. Connect the task to a household or community situation you know.

slides.title: Find help that fits your version
slides.body: Use the app’s Help menu or official support. State the task, what you tried and the exact error. Ask a partner for one specific improvement.

slides.title: Knowledge check: the wrong speaker
slides.body: The video is playing silently. What should you check first?
options: Restart the computer
Check the output device and mute
Turn the volume all the way up
slides.why: The selected output device or mute setting may explain the silence. Change one thing and test.

slides.title: Knowledge check: calendar privacy
slides.body: A partner only needs to know when you are free. Which sharing option best fits?
options: Share every event detail
Make the calendar public
Share free/busy availability
slides.why: Availability answers the scheduling question while limiting event details. A public calendar can show details to anyone.

slides.title: Lab: your usable workstation
slides.body: Complete the worksheet. Show your partner the result of one setting change, a calendar entry and a print preview.

slides.title: Keep the routine
slides.body: Choose a setting, test it and explain the result. Before leaving, save your practice work and restore shared settings.

lab: Record one task you want to make easier and one skill you bring.
Increase webpage text with browser zoom (Ctrl and +). Record the control you used, then reset it with Ctrl and 0.
Select the headset as the sound output and play a test sound. Record where the brightness control is for your screen, and explain brightness versus contrast.
Match HDMI, Ethernet and USB to three jobs: an external screen, a wired network and a flash drive. Find one real port on your computer.

Create a fictional library appointment: title, day, start and end, place and a reminder. If no calendar app is set up, write the same five fields here on paper, as in video chapter 7, and mark it simulated. Reread it and check each field.
Choose a calendar view and a sharing level for a partner who only needs availability. Explain why.
Open print preview (Ctrl and P) for page 1 of this worksheet. Record the printer name, orientation and pages. Set Pages to 1 and Copies to 1. Do not print unless the instructor directs it.
In Word, type teh and a space; autocorrect changes it to the. Press Ctrl and Z to undo it. Record a useful help search and one piece of partner feedback.
answers: Accept a personally meaningful goal and existing skill.
Browser zoom (Ctrl and +) or the page’s text-size control; demonstrates reset with Ctrl and 0.
Headset selected and tested; mute checked. Brightness is light output (monitor buttons on a desktop); contrast is light/dark separation.
External screen: HDMI. Wired network: Ethernet. Flash drive: USB. USB-C features vary by device and cable.
Title, day, start/end, location, reminder; time zone when relevant. A paper entry marked simulated is acceptable when no calendar account is set up.
Week for conflicts; free/busy for limited detail. Verify service-specific options.
Printer name matches the lab destination; Pages 1 and Copies 1; orientation recorded; nothing printed without direction.
Autocorrect changed teh to the and Ctrl and Z restored it; the learner checks suggestions rather than trusting them; the help search names the app and task.
outcomes: Settings: at a lab workstation with Edge, each learner enlarges a webpage with browser zoom and returns it to 100% (Ctrl and 0), selects the headset as the sound output and confirms it with a test, and names which control (page zoom, display scale or brightness) fits a described reading problem. All three are correct with no more than one prompt, and lab settings are restored.

Calendar: using a calendar form (a demonstration account or the paper form from video chapter 7), each learner creates a fictional event with title, day, start and end, place and reminder, rereads it to confirm all five, and chooses free/busy sharing for a partner, explaining what the partner will see.

Connections and printing: given three jobs (external screen, wired network, flash drive), each learner matches HDMI, Ethernet and USB and finds one real port, then opens print preview for page 1 of the worksheet, confirms the printer name, and sets Pages to 1 and Copies to 1 without printing.
Automation: in Word, each learner triggers an AutoCorrect change (teh to the), undoes it with Ctrl and Z, and says in one sentence what a mail rule and a cloud service do.
Help: each learner writes a help request that names the app, the task, what they tried and the exact message, and records one specific piece of partner feedback.
weeks.prep: Each station: a headset, Microsoft Edge, Microsoft Word, and this lesson and worksheet. At the front: an HDMI, a USB and an Ethernet cable to hold up, and the projector showing Edge. The lab has no calendar account, so worksheet task 5 uses the paper form from video chapter 7 unless you set up a demonstration account. Decide before class whether one test print is allowed. Play video chapters 2 and 7 with captions to check sound. After your own run-through, select Start fresh on this computer at each station. Keep 3–5 printed pre-tests in case the network fails. No paid service, real purchase or new learner account is required.
lab_paths: Zoom a webpage
Press Ctrl and + to zoom in, Ctrl and - to zoom out, and Ctrl and 0 to reset. Or open the browser menu (··· in Edge, ⋮ in Chrome) and use Zoom.
Make everything bigger
Start › Settings › System › Display. Under Scale & layout, choose a size from Scale.
Make only text bigger
Start › Settings › Accessibility › Text size. Drag the slider, then select Apply.
Choose the sound output
Select the speaker icon on the taskbar, then the arrow next to the volume slider, and choose the headset. Or Start › Settings › System › Sound › Output.
Mute or unmute
Select the speaker icon on the taskbar, then the speaker symbol at the left of the volume slider.
Screen brightness
Desktop monitor: use the buttons on the monitor. Laptop: select the sound or battery icon on the taskbar to open Quick Settings, then drag Brightness.
Easier-to-read colors
Start › Settings › Accessibility › Contrast themes. Choose a theme, then select Apply.
Browser downloads and site permissions
Open Settings from the browser menu (··· in Edge, ⋮ in Chrome), then type downloads or permissions in the Search settings box.
Check a printer and its queue
Start › Settings › Bluetooth & devices › Printers & scanners › Open print queue. Pick your printer from the Printers menu in that window.
Set a default printer
In Printers & scanners, turn off Let Windows manage my default printer, then select Set as default next to the printer’s name.
Print preview
Press Ctrl and P. Check Printer, Pages, Copies and Layout before you select Print.
Share free/busy only

Outlook.com: Calendar › Share › enter the person’s email › Can view when I’m busy. Google Calendar: Settings › Settings for my calendars › your calendar › Share with specific people or groups › See only free/busy (hide details).
Undo an autocorrect change in Word
Type teh and a space; Word changes it to the. Press Ctrl and Z right away to undo. Settings: File › Options › Proofing › AutoCorrect Options.

weeks.title: Find, judge, and organize information
weeks.summary: Find a reliable community resource and manage a shared file with care.
objectives: Ask a search tool a full-sentence question that names the service, the place and one detail, then refine it with a follow-up.
Read an AI answer as a lead, check it against the organization's own page, and record where you found it.
Fill in an online form with only what is needed, and read the confirmation.
Save a file with a clear name in a folder you can find, and pack it in a ZIP file.
Choose who can view, comment or edit, and pick the right way to get a file back.
agenda: Opening video

Play the opening video, starting at chapter 1 (7:35 in all, captions on). It asks learners to ask well, check the answer, and keep a source trail, then Cycles A to D replay the chapters they need. Pause only if a question comes up.
Welcome, experience and overview
Logins. Pairs share last week's home task. Read the overview: four missions, each with extra rounds, then a capstone.
Cycle A: ask well, then check it

Tell: full-sentence questions; an AI answer is a lead; open the source. Show: chapters 2 and 3, pausing at 1:26 so learners say a question aloud and at 2:22 so they name one detail the page confirms, then chapter 4 (leave a source trail); then live in Edge, ask a question about a local library, a follow-up, then open the library's own page. Do: worksheet tasks 1 to 4 and the rounds rescue the weak question, catch the error and safe to ask, every learner at their own seat. Review: the library answer says 9 but its page says 8; a partner explains the next step.
Cycle B: complete a form carefully

Tell: the practice form. Show: chapter 5, pausing at 3:41 before chapter 6 starts; then show the message Please select an item in the list. Do: worksheet task 5 and the rounds needed, ask why first or do not give, then read before you send, every learner. Review: what the practice confirmation does not prove.
Cycle C: organize and recover a file

Tell: folder, file name, ZIP and Recycle Bin. Show: chapter 6, then live in File Explorer and Word. Do: worksheet task 6 and the rounds rename the mess, find it fast and which tool fixes it, every learner. Review: the file exists but a paragraph was replaced; a partner names the tool.
Cycle D: share only the access needed

Tell: Viewer, Commenter, Editor; sync versus backup. Show: chapter 7, pausing at 5:14 before the answer so learners choose the role; chapter 8 (optional pause at 5:59) and chapter 9. Do: worksheet tasks 7 and 8 and the rounds role cards and delete it, then what, every learner. Review: the neighbor only needs to read the handout.
Capstone: community resource folder

Each learner picks a new service, asks a question, checks one source, writes the five-field note, saves it in Community resources, ZIPs the folder and plans the access. Partners swap the note only and test whether the trail can be followed.
Individual check

Play chapter 10 and pause at 6:47 to ask what the folder should hold; play on to compare. Each learner shows the five-field source note, the file reopened from Community resources, and a file restored from the Recycle Bin, and names the role for a reviewer. Mark Independent, With prompt or Needs practice on the roster.
Apply and close

Home task: ask one question about a service you need, check one source and write the five-field note, kept in a named folder; share it at the start of week 3. Print or save the worksheet, delete the Community resources folder and ZIP from Documents, then select Start fresh on this computer.

slides.title: Start with a question
slides.body: You need a local library’s computer-help service. What information would make the answer usable?

slides.title: Ask the way you would ask a person
slides.body: Say what you need, where you are and one detail that matters. Where can I get free computer help near Beckley, WV, in the evening? is a better question than computer help.

slides.title: Read the answer as a lead
slides.body: An AI answer, such as an AI Overview, is a quick summary written from many pages. It can sound sure and still be wrong, out of date or about a different town. Treat it as a lead, not a source.

slides.title: Open the source behind the answer
slides.body: Open the organization's own page. Ask who published it, when it was updated and whether it fits your question. If the page and the AI answer disagree, trust the page.

slides.title: Compare two results
slides.body: An AI answer can link to many pages. These are fictional practice sources. Select a card, then say which page you would open and check first.
cards: Library service page
Named library, contact method, service hours and update note. Verify details through its official contact.
Unattributed social post
No author or date; promises every service is free everywhere. Treat the claim as unverified.

slides.title: When the answer and the page disagree
slides.body: If the AI answer and the page disagree, trust the organization that runs the service, and confirm hours by phone before you travel.

slides.title: Keep a source trail
slides.body: Record the title, organization, address, access date and the specific detail you used. If an AI answer led you to the page, record the page it pointed to, not the summary.

slides.title: Collect only what the task needs
slides.body: Forms and surveys collect responses into a shared system. Identify who collects the data, why, and which fields are required before typing.

slides.title: Practice form: request computer help
slides.body: Use fictional details in this local practice form. Check required fields, review your choices and read the confirmation.

slides.title: Name files so you can find them
slides.body: Use a clear subject and version: library-help-v1.docx. Keep related files in one folder, such as Community resources. Avoid names such as final-final-new.

slides.title: Central storage needs clear access
slides.body: A shared drive keeps one common copy in one place. The service, account or organization controls who can open it and how long it is kept. Sharing a link does not make someone the owner.

slides.title: Sync, backup, and recovery
slides.body: Sync copies changes, including deletions, between your computer and an online service. A backup is a separate copy kept somewhere else. Version history, kept by services such as OneDrive and Google Docs, may bring back earlier wording.

slides.title: Watch: search, judge, share, recover
slides.body: Follow the worked examples, pause for practice, and choose a chapter to replay a skill. Connect the task to a household or community situation you know.

slides.title: Choose who can change the file
slides.body: A viewer reads. A commenter suggests, where the service offers it. An editor changes content. Google Drive says Viewer, Commenter and Editor; OneDrive says Can view and Can edit. Give each named person the least access the task needs.

slides.title: Read-only is not encryption
slides.body: Read-only stops changes, but the file can still be read and copied. Encryption scrambles the content so only someone with the password or key can read it. A password to open and a password to modify protect different things.

slides.title: Compression packages files
slides.body: A ZIP file bundles several files into one and can make them smaller to send. Extract it before editing. Photos and video are often already compressed. A ZIP file is not encryption or a backup.

slides.title: Recover the right thing
slides.body: Missing file? Check the Recycle Bin or the service's recycle bin. Wrong wording? Use version history, which needs a service such as OneDrive or Google Docs. Preview first and tell collaborators before restoring.

slides.title: Knowledge check: a credible page
slides.body: An AI answer makes a surprising claim about a service. Which action best checks it?
options: Trust it because the AI answer sounds sure
Trust it because several websites repeat it
Open the organization's own page and check it
slides.why: The organization's own page is the evidence. An answer that sounds sure, or many sites repeating it, does not check the claim.

slides.title: Knowledge check: read-only
slides.body: A file is read-only. What does that tell you?
options: Editing is restricted
The content is encrypted
Nobody can copy the content
slides.why: Read-only describes an editing restriction. It does not by itself prove confidentiality or prevent copying.

slides.title: Lab: build a resource folder
slides.body: Do each worksheet task in its cycle. Save your file in the Community resources folder. Mark sharing and version history as simulated.

slides.title: Your repeatable information routine
slides.body: Ask a clear question, check the source, save the evidence and limit access.

lab: Write a question about a local public service you or a neighbor might need, such as computer help at a public library. Name the service, the town and one detail that matters to you, such as evening hours.
In Edge, ask Google your question. Read the answer, then ask one follow-up question. Record your question and what the follow-up changed. Do not type any private details.

Open one source link beside or beneath the answer. Record the page title, the organization, the web address (Ctrl and L, Ctrl and C, then Ctrl and V here), today's date and the one detail you will use.

For that page, answer three checks in a few words each: who published it, when it was updated, and whether it fits your question. Name one detail in the AI answer that the page does not confirm, and one detail to confirm with the organization.

On the Mission 2B practice page, select Review practice request with one choice left blank, and write the message you see. Then choose a topic and a contact method, submit, and copy the confirmation. Say what the confirmation does not prove.

Open File Explorer (Windows logo key and E) › Documents. Make a folder named Community resources. In Word, type your task 1 question and task 3 source note, and save the file in that folder as library-help-v1.docx. Close Word, reopen the file from the folder, and say who controls a copy kept in a cloud drive.

On the Mission 2D practice page, choose access for three people: one who only reads, one who suggests wording, and one who writes the handout with you. Record each role and why, and mark it simulated. Say what read-only does and does not do.

Right-click Community resources › Show more options › Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder. Right-click the ZIP file › Extract All, then open the extracted file. Delete that file and restore it from the Recycle Bin. On the Mission 2C practice page, choose the route for wrong wording and mark it simulated.
answers: The question names a service, a town and one detail, for example: Where can I get free computer help at a public library in Beckley, WV, in the evening?

A full-sentence question with no private details. One follow-up (for example Which are open Saturdays?) and what it changed, such as a shorter or more local list. The AI answer is treated as a lead, not as proof.
All five fields: page title, organization, full web address, date checked and one specific detail, taken from the organization's own page rather than from the AI summary. No personal records.

Who published it (credibility), when it was updated (current), and whether it fits the question (relevance), each tied to something on the page. One detail in the AI answer that the page does not confirm, and one detail, such as hours or eligibility, to confirm through the organization's own contact.
Message: Please select an item in the list. Confirmation: Practice complete … No request was sent. It shows the exercise was done, not that anyone received a request.

Documents › Community resources holds library-help-v1.docx, reopened from that folder. The service and account (or the organization) control a cloud copy; the person who shares a file stays the owner.

Reader: Viewer. Reviewer: Commenter, or the nearest option the service offers. Co-writer: Editor. Named people and the least access each task needs, marked simulated. Read-only stops changes but the file can still be read and copied; it is not encryption.

The ZIP file holds the folder and the extracted file opens. The deleted file is back in its folder from the Recycle Bin. Wrong wording: version history (simulated; it needs a service such as OneDrive or Google Docs). Missing file: the Recycle Bin or the service's recycle bin. Backup: a separate copy for when every synced copy is gone. A ZIP packages files; it is not encryption or a backup.
lab_paths: Ask a full-sentence question

Press Ctrl and L, type your question as you would ask a person (the service, the place and one detail) and press Enter. Google may show an AI Overview above the results. If an AI Mode button or tab appears, select it to keep asking follow-up questions.
Ask a follow-up
Type a short follow-up in the same place, such as: Which of these are open on Saturdays? You do not need to start over.
Open the source behind an answer
Look for links beside or beneath the answer and open the organization's own page. Check who published it and when it was updated.
Keep private details out of a question
Do not type a Social Security number, bank or card number, password, claim number or health details into a question.
Find a word on a long page
Press Ctrl and F, then type the word you want to find on the page.
Copy a web address into your notes
Press Ctrl and L to select the address, then Ctrl and C to copy it. Click in your notes and press Ctrl and V to paste.
Make a new folder
Press the Windows logo key and E to open File Explorer. Open Documents, select New › Folder, type the name and press Enter. Or press Ctrl and Shift and N.
Save a Word file into that folder
In Word, select File › Save As › Browse. Open Documents › Community resources, type the File name, then select Save.
Rename a file
In File Explorer, select the file and press F2, or right-click it and select Rename. Type the new name and press Enter.
Make a ZIP file
Right-click the folder, then select Show more options › Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder. The ZIP file appears next to the folder.
Open the files in a ZIP
Right-click the ZIP file, select Extract All, then follow the steps. Open the files from the new folder, not from inside the ZIP.
Get back a deleted file
Open the Recycle Bin on the desktop, right-click the file and select Restore. It returns to its folder. Shift and Delete skips the Recycle Bin.
Protect a Word file (instructor shows)
File › Info › Protect Document. Always Open Read-Only limits changes; Encrypt with Password asks for a password to open. Word cannot recover a lost password.
Share or see earlier versions (instructor shows; needs an account)

OneDrive: select the file › Share, then choose Can view or Can edit; right-click the file › Version history. Google Drive: Share › Viewer, Commenter or Editor; in a Google Doc, select Last edit at the top right to see versions.
weeks.prep: Each station: Microsoft Edge, Microsoft Word (Notepad works if Word is missing; save as library-help-v1.txt), File Explorer with a local Documents folder that is not signed in to OneDrive, headphones, and this lesson and worksheet. At the front: the projector showing Edge, File Explorer and Word, and one real West Virginia public library page for the source demonstration, checked the day before. The lab has no cloud account for learners, so sharing (worksheet task 7) and version history (task 8) use the Mission 2D and Mission 2C practice pages, marked simulated; if you have your own OneDrive or Google account, you may show the Share box and version history on the projector with a fictional file only. No printing is needed; decide whether learners may print their worksheet or should save it as a PDF before closing. Play video chapters 2, 6 and 7 with captions to check sound, and mark the pause points 1:26, 2:22, 3:41, 5:14 and 6:47. Google shows an AI Overview for some questions only, and AI Mode may not appear for every learner: rehearse your demonstration question the day before, and use the fictional AI answer on the worksheet (Mission A, Round 3) if no AI answer appears. No sign-in is needed. After your own run-through, delete your practice folder and ZIP from Documents and select Start fresh on this computer at each station. No paid service, real purchase or new learner account is required.
outcomes: Search: in Microsoft Edge at a lab workstation, given a local service need, each learner asks Google a full-sentence question that names the service, the place and one detail, asks one follow-up, and says in one sentence what the follow-up changed. No private details typed. Correct with no more than one prompt.

Sources: for one source link from that answer, each learner records the five source fields (title, organization, web address, date checked and the detail used), answers the three source checks (who published it, when it was updated, whether it fits), and names one detail in the AI answer that the page does not confirm. All five fields are present and each judgment points to something on the page.

Forms: using the practice form on the Mission 2B practice page with fictional details, each learner submits once with a required choice missing, reads the message, completes the form, and explains that the confirmation does not mean anyone received a request.

Files: in File Explorer at a lab workstation, each learner makes a folder named Community resources, saves a Word file in it as library-help-v1.docx, reopens it from that folder, compresses the folder to a ZIP file, extracts it and opens the extracted copy. All steps done, with nothing saved in the wrong place.

Access and recovery: using the permission practice on the Mission 2D practice page (simulated), each learner chooses Viewer, Commenter or Editor for a reader, a reviewer and a co-writer, giving each the least access the task needs; restores a deleted practice file from the Recycle Bin; says when version history is the right tool instead; and says that read-only stops changes but is not encryption. All correct with no more than one prompt.

weeks.title: Create something people can use
weeks.summary: Build a clear resource handout, a small workbook, and a short presentation.
objectives: Give a handout real headings, numbered steps and a clear link.
Use shortcuts and Track Changes to edit safely and let the owner decide.
Add costs with a SUM formula and check that the total updates.
Make three matching slides with a cropped, described and credited photo.
Save a PDF, check it, and choose the right file type for the next person.

slides.title: Create for someone specific
slides.body: Your audience is a neighbor looking for computer help. What would they need first, and what can you leave out?

slides.title: A document needs structure
slides.body: Use a descriptive title, real heading styles, short sections and a numbered list of steps. Bold text only looks like a heading. Screen readers (software that reads the screen aloud) and Word's Navigation pane find real headings, not bold.

slides.title: Keyboard shortcuts with a purpose
slides.body: Ctrl+C copies; Ctrl+V pastes; Ctrl+Z undoes; Ctrl+S saves; Ctrl+K adds a link. Select only the text you want to change first. On a Mac at home, use Command instead of Ctrl.

slides.title: Make one clear paragraph
slides.body: State the service, who it helps and the next action. Read it aloud. Replace vague words with concrete instructions.

slides.title: Track a proposed change
slides.body: In Word, select Review › Track Changes, then make one edit. It shows as a suggestion. The document's owner selects Accept or Reject; a comment can explain why. Google Docs calls this Suggesting.

slides.title: Prepare a handout someone can read
slides.body: Use real headings, readable type and link text that names the destination. Give each informative picture alternative text (alt text): a short description that screen-reading software reads aloud. Right-click the picture and choose View Alt Text. Do not rely on color alone.

slides.title: A workbook has rows, columns, and cells
slides.body: A row can represent one item; a column can represent a category. Label the units. Keep numbers as numbers so formulas can calculate.

slides.title: Build a fictional supply budget
slides.body: Open supplies.csv in Excel. Click B5 and type =SUM(B2:B4). The equals sign starts a formula, and the colon means through: B2 through B4. Press Enter. B5 shows 25.

slides.title: Check the formula, not just the appearance
slides.body: Predict first: what will B5 show if paper costs 15? Then type 15 in B2 and press Enter. The total should become 28. If it stays at 25, check the range and whether a number was typed as text.

slides.title: A chart answers a question
slides.body: A bar chart can compare costs. In Excel, select A1:B4, then Insert › Recommended Charts. Give it a title with units, and keep the table so no one has to judge by color.

slides.title: Three slides; one useful message
slides.body: Slide 1: the need. Slide 2: the steps. Slide 3: where to get help. Pick one theme on the Design tab so all three match, and keep text large enough for the back of the room.

slides.title: Crop, resize, and preserve the original
slides.body: Crop trims the outer edges. Resize changes the size. In PowerPoint, select the picture, then Picture Format › Crop. To resize without stretching, hold Shift and drag a corner. The photo file on your computer does not change. Keep the creator's credit.

slides.title: Basic video editing
slides.body: Trim removes unwanted material at the start or end. Split lets you remove a middle section. Keep speech clear and check that captions still match. The Windows video editor, Clipchamp, needs a Microsoft account, so practice on this slide.

slides.title: Watch: create, check, and export
slides.body: Follow the worked examples, pause for practice, and choose a chapter to replay a skill. Connect the task to a household or community situation you know.

slides.title: Reusing content requires permission
slides.body: Check the license and its conditions. Credit the creator, title, source and license when required. An image appearing in search does not mean you may reuse it.

slides.title: Choose a format for the next person
slides.body: An editable document supports revision. PDF keeps a finished layout. CSV keeps plain values only: saving a workbook as CSV drops its formulas and formatting.
cards: A neighbor needs a handout
PDF, then check reading order and legibility.
A partner must edit paragraphs
An editable document with appropriate access.
A tool needs plain rows and columns

slides.title: Inspect the export
slides.body: Open the PDF from its folder, not from Word. Check headings, page breaks, links and missing content. Check the file name and folder. The PDF is a separate file, so test it on its own.

slides.title: Knowledge check: a changing total
slides.body: Which formula adds the values in B2, B3 and B4?
options: =SUM(B2,B4)
=SUM(B2:B4)
SUM(B2:B4)
slides.why: The equals sign starts a formula, and the colon means through, so B2:B4 adds B2, B3 and B4. A comma adds only the cells it lists. Without the equals sign, Excel treats it as text.

slides.title: Knowledge check: a proposed edit
slides.body: You want to reword one step in a partner's handout and let the owner keep or undo your wording with one click. What should you use?
options: Type over the step
Turn on Track Changes
Email a changed copy
slides.why: Track Changes shows your edit as a suggestion, and the owner selects Accept or Reject. Typing over hides what changed; a changed copy makes the owner compare by eye.

slides.title: Lab: your resource pack
slides.body: Open the worksheet now and keep it open. Do each task right after its demonstration. Save every file in your Resource pack folder in Documents.

slides.title: Useful beats elaborate
slides.body: A clear structure, a correct calculation and a tested export serve your audience.

lab: Who will read a computer-help handout, and what should they do after reading it? Write one sentence that names the reader and the next action.

In Word, open a blank document and type these lines, one per line: Computer help at the library / Who it helps / Anyone who wants to practice one computer task. / Steps / Choose one task. / Visit the learning desk. / Ask how to repeat it at home. Make the first line Heading 1, and Who it helps and Steps Heading 2 (Home › Styles). Select the three steps and choose Home › Numbering. Open View › Navigation Pane and check that both headings are listed.

Add a last line: Read the computer-help guide. Select it, press Ctrl and K, type https://example.org/help in the Address box and select OK. Select the words learning desk, press Ctrl and C, click at the end of the last line, press Ctrl and V, then Ctrl and Z to undo. Save the file as resource-handout in your Resource pack folder. Record the shortcut that helped most.

Swap seats with your partner. In their handout, select Review › Track Changes and change one word to make a step clearer. Swap back. Find your partner's change, select Review › Accept or Reject, and write your reason.

Download supplies.csv (button below) and open it in Excel. Click B1 and type Cost in dollars. Type Total in A5. Click B5, type =SUM(B2:B4) and press Enter; B5 should show 25. Before you change anything, write what B5 will show if paper costs 15.
Click B2, type 15 and press Enter, then check B5 against your prediction. Save with File › Save As as an Excel Workbook named supplies in your Resource pack folder.

In PowerPoint, choose Blank Presentation and pick one theme on the Design tab. Make three slides titled Need computer help? / Steps / Where to get help. Paste the three steps from your handout on the second slide, and type Visit the learning desk on the third slide. Check the words can be read from the back of the room. Save as resource-slides in your Resource pack folder.

Download the practice photo (button below). On the first slide, choose Insert › Pictures › This Device and insert it. Select Picture Format › Crop, drag the black handles in so the two people and the handout fill the picture, and press Esc. Right-click the photo, choose View Alt Text, and write one sentence about what it shows. Type this credit in the subtitle box: Photo: VUB practice photo, used with permission. Save.

In Word, save the handout as a PDF: File › Save a Copy (or Save As) › Browse, open Resource pack, set Save as type to PDF and select Save. Open Resource pack in File Explorer and double-click the PDF. Check the headings, numbered steps and link. Write which format fits a neighbor who only reads it, a partner who must edit it, and a tool that needs plain rows.
answers: Names a specific reader (for example, a neighbor who wants computer help) and one next action (for example, visit the learning desk).
The first line uses Heading 1, and Who it helps and Steps use Heading 2, not bold; the three steps are numbered; both headings appear in the Navigation pane.
The link text names the destination and the link opens; paste and undo worked with no lost text; resource-handout is in the Resource pack folder; one useful shortcut is named.
The edit appeared as a tracked change before the owner selected Accept or Reject; the reason names what the reader needs. Only the owner makes the final choice.
B1 reads Cost in dollars; B5 shows =SUM(B2:B4) in the formula bar and 25; a written prediction came before any change.
B5 shows 28 after B2 becomes 15; the file is saved as supplies.xlsx. Saving as CSV would keep the number but drop the formula.
Three slides in the order need, steps, help; one theme on all three; text readable from the back of the room; the steps match the handout.
The photo is cropped in PowerPoint and the photo file itself is unchanged; the alt text says in one sentence what the photo shows; the credit line names the source and the permission.
The PDF is in Resource pack and opens; the checks name headings, steps and a working link; a reader gets the PDF, an editor the Word document, and a tool that needs rows gets CSV.

slides.title: Choose a channel for the task
slides.body: A quick status update, a detailed request and an urgent issue may need different channels. Consider the audience, sensitivity and response time.

slides.title: Personal and professional identities
slides.body: Use the account and tone that fit your role, and check which account is active before you post or send. Use a different password for each account. A password manager is an app that stores them safely. Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds a second check, such as a text code.

slides.title: Write an email someone can act on
slides.body: Use a specific subject, a greeting, one clear request, needed context and a courteous close. Check the recipient and attachment before sending.

slides.title: To, Cc, and Bcc
slides.body: To names the person who should act. Cc sends a copy that everyone can see. Bcc hides those addresses from the others; it does not encrypt the message or stop forwarding. Reply all goes to the sender and everyone in To and Cc, so check who needs your answer.

slides.title: Timing changes how a message lands
slides.body: Say when you need a reply, and consider urgency and the reader’s working hours. Scheduled send lets you write now and choose when the message goes out, such as 9 a.m. tomorrow. It will not fix unclear wording, so check the message and the time first.

slides.title: Inclusive language helps people respond
slides.body: Use the name and form of address people prefer. Explain unfamiliar abbreviations. Avoid assumptions about age, culture, abilities or technology experience.

slides.title: Participate in a community
slides.body: Read the group’s guidelines, stay on topic and disagree with ideas respectfully. Ask permission before sharing someone else’s story or image.

slides.title: Verify a community service
slides.body: Use an organization’s official contact or website to confirm eligibility, availability and hours. A directory entry is a starting point; details can change.

slides.title: Collaborate on one shared copy
slides.body: Working together lets each person add what they know and catch mistakes. Assign an owner, writer and reviewer. Agree where the one shared file lives, such as OneDrive or Google Drive, and what finished means. Clear roles reduce conflicting edits.

slides.title: Live editing or later feedback?
slides.body: Synchronous work happens together. Asynchronous work happens at different times. Match the method to schedules and the decision needed.
cards: Write together during class
Synchronous coauthoring in one shared Word or Google Docs file: agree who edits which section.
Review after class
Asynchronous comments in the same file, or an email: include enough context for the writer.

slides.title: Feedback names an improvement
slides.body: Try: “The contact method is hard to find. Could we put it after the steps?” Be specific about the text, reason and possible change.

slides.title: Acknowledge and resolve
slides.body: Read a comment, ask if unclear, make or decline the change with a reason, then resolve it. A resolved comment is hidden, not deleted. For a file saved online, such as in OneDrive, version history can bring back a lost edit.

slides.title: Meetings and webinars
slides.body: Test sound before you join. Mute when not speaking. Use raise hand or chat as the host asks, and turn on captions if they help. Ask before recording. In a webinar the host controls who can speak, so ask questions in Q&A or chat.

slides.title: Watch: collaborate without confusion
slides.body: Follow the worked examples, pause for practice, and choose a chapter to replay a skill. Connect the task to a household or community situation you know.

slides.title: Goods, services, and subscriptions
slides.body: Goods are products; services provide work or access. Streaming plays video or music over the internet as you watch or listen: Netflix, YouTube and Spotify are examples, and hoopla is free with a West Virginia library card. A subscription can keep renewing until you cancel it.

slides.title: Review a digital payment
slides.body: Know how you pay. A credit card lets you dispute a wrong charge. A digital wallet, such as Apple Pay or Google Pay, pays with a card you saved. Money sent with Zelle, Venmo or Cash App is hard to get back, so pay only people you know. Check the seller, total and refund terms first.

slides.title: Small in-app purchases add up
slides.body: A free app may sell extras, and a saved card makes each one a single tap. Turn on a password or approval for purchases, and check your receipts. Deleting an app does not cancel its subscription. Do not buy anything during this activity.

slides.title: Knowledge check: useful feedback
slides.body: Which comment best supports revision?
options: Nice work! The handout looks good to me as it is.
In step 2, name the room so readers know where to go.
Step 2 is confusing and needs to be much clearer.
slides.why: It names the place (step 2), the change (name the room) and the reason (readers can find it). Praise alone or a vague complaint gives the writer nothing to act on.

slides.title: Knowledge check: a trial offer
slides.body: Before starting a free trial, what should you check?
options: Only that the first seven days cost nothing
The renewal price, renewal date and how to cancel
That deleting the app later will stop the charges
slides.why: A free trial usually becomes a paid plan unless you cancel the way the seller says. Deleting the app does not cancel the subscription.

slides.title: Lab: coordinate a small team
slides.body: Show your instructor three things: your To, Cc and Bcc choices, a comment you answered and resolved, and your offer comparison with a way to pay.

slides.title: Leave a clear next step
slides.body: A useful message says who needs to do what and when. A useful review helps the next person act.

lab: Choose a channel for each message and explain the difference: (a) a detailed request that your partner can answer tomorrow; (b) an urgent problem in this room right now.

In the box below, write a practice email to a fictional reviewer, Sam, asking for comments on the computer-help handout. Pat organizes the Saturday session and should see it. Include To, Cc, a specific subject, a greeting, one clear request, when you need a reply, and a courteous close. Nothing is sent.

You are sending a notice about the fictional Saturday computer-help session. Alex runs the session, Pat organizes it and should see the notice, and 20 volunteers should not see one another’s addresses. Write who goes in To, Cc and Bcc. If Pat clicks Reply all, who receives it? Choose a time to schedule the notice, and say whether it should come from your personal account or the volunteer group’s account.
Rewrite this message so anyone can follow it: “Pls turn on MFA ASAP. Even older folks can manage it.” Spell out each abbreviation, give a clear time, and remove the assumption about age.

With your partner, choose who is owner, writer and reviewer for the handout. Say where the one shared copy would live and what access each person needs (viewer, commenter or editor). Would you edit together now (synchronous) or leave comments for later (asynchronous)? Explain why. This is a decision; no file is shared.

In Word, type the title “How to get computer help” and two steps: 1. Choose a task. 2. Visit the learning desk. Swap seats: on your partner’s handout, select one step, choose Review, then New Comment, and write a comment that names the place, the change and the reason. Swap back: reply to the comment on your handout, make or decline the change, then resolve it. Record your comment and your decision here. Leave Word open for the final check.

Open the Mission 4C practice page. In the practice meeting, unmute, raise your hand, lower it, then mute again. If your headset has a microphone, test it (see the quick card row Test your headset microphone). Then list four meeting or webinar habits, including asking before recording, and one detail you would confirm with the organization itself before trusting a community post.

Compare two fictional offers for a streaming TV service. Offer A: free for 30 days, then $6 a month until you cancel. Offer B: $60 a year, paid now, renews every year. What does A cost for 3 months? For 12 months? Write two questions to ask before you start a free trial. Which would you use to pay a website you have not used before: a credit card, a debit card, a digital wallet or a person-to-person app such as Zelle in your bank’s app, Venmo or Cash App? Explain why. Do not open a real store.
answers: (a) A written message, such as email, with the details and a link to the shared handout, so the partner can answer later. (b) Tell the instructor in person now, because it is urgent and here. A phone call or text suits an urgent problem outside the room.

To: Sam. Cc: Pat. A subject that names the task (for example, Please review the computer-help handout by Thursday); a greeting; one clear request; a reply-by time (for example, by Thursday at 3 p.m.); a courteous close. A partner reading it can say what to do and by when. The worksheet draft counts as a simulated email.

To: Alex. Cc: Pat. Bcc: the 20 volunteers, so their addresses stay hidden. Pat’s Reply all goes to you and Alex only; Bcc recipients do not receive a Reply all. Schedule it for working hours, such as 9 a.m. on a weekday. Send it from the volunteer group’s account. Bcc does not encrypt the message or stop forwarding.

For example: “Please turn on multifactor authentication (MFA), a second sign-in check such as a text code, by Friday. I am happy to help if you would like.” Both abbreviations are spelled out or removed, a clear time replaces ASAP, and nothing assumes age or ability.

Owner coordinates and sets access (editor); writer edits (editor); reviewer comments (commenter). One agreed copy, for example in OneDrive or Google Drive. Synchronous when everyone can work at the same time; asynchronous comments when schedules differ. A decision with a reason is enough; real sharing needs an account.

The comment names a place, a change and a reason (for example, In step 2, add where the desk is, Room A on the first floor, so first-time visitors can find it). The writer replies, makes or declines the change with a reason, and resolves the comment only after that. The comment shows the station’s Word user name, not the reviewer’s.

The practice meeting is used correctly, and the microphone test shows sound if the headset has a microphone. Habits: test sound first, mute when not speaking, use raise hand, chat or Q&A as the host asks, turn on captions if helpful, ask before recording. In a webinar, attendees usually cannot unmute. Community check: hours, eligibility or cost, confirmed through the organization’s official website or phone number.

A: $12 for 3 months (2 paid months after the free month) and $66 for 12 months (11 paid months). B: $60 whether you keep it 3 or 12 months, so B is cheaper only if you keep it a full year. Questions: when does the trial end and what will it cost then, how do I cancel, are there refunds, who is the seller? Payment: a credit card, or a digital wallet that uses one, because a wrong or unauthorized charge can be disputed. A person-to-person app is for people you know; money sent is hard to get back. No real purchase or payment details.
lab_paths: Check which account you are using

In a new email, read the From line: it shows the account the message will come from. Outlook.com and Gmail also show the signed-in account behind the picture at the top right. The Edge profile picture shows the browser profile, which can differ from the mail account.
Add Cc or Bcc to an email
Outlook.com: in a new message, select Cc or Bcc on the right side of the To line. New Outlook app: Options › Show fields › Show Bcc. Gmail: in a new message, select Cc or Bcc on the To line.
Reply or Reply all
Reply goes only to the sender. Reply all goes to the sender and everyone on the To and Cc lines, never to Bcc. Check the list before you select Send.
Schedule an email
Outlook.com or new Outlook: select the arrow next to Send, then Schedule send, and pick a time. Gmail: select the arrow next to Send, then Schedule send. Check the time zone.
Add a comment in Word

slides.title: Safety is a set of decisions
slides.body: Choose one habit that protects your work and one that helps you use technology comfortably.

slides.title: A comfortable workstation
slides.body: Set the screen about an arm’s length away, with the top at or slightly below eye level. Keep the keyboard and mouse close. Change position and take short breaks, and ask for help with discomfort that does not go away.

slides.title: Universal design helps more people
slides.body: Universal design means building tools that more people can use without special changes. Captions help in a noisy room or with hearing loss. Keyboard access helps people who cannot use a mouse, and clear text labels help people who cannot tell some colors apart.

slides.title: Protect attention and wellbeing
slides.body: FOMO means fear of missing out: the pull to keep checking so you do not miss anything. Choose which alerts you really need. Do not disturb can quiet the rest while you finish a task.

slides.title: An online identity can be invented
slides.body: Catfishing is using a fake identity to build trust, sometimes with stolen photos of real service members. Pressure for money, secrecy or personal information is a reason to pause and verify another way. Never send money or gift cards to someone you have not met in person.

slides.title: Respond to harmful posts
slides.body: Avoid escalating. Preserve evidence when safe, use reporting or blocking tools and seek support. Negative posts can affect real relationships and future opportunities.

slides.title: An urgent message is not proof
slides.body: Phishing is a fake message posing as a trusted organization. Warning signs: pressure to act now, a mismatched sender or link, a request for a password or money. Check through the real website or a number you trust. Typed a password already? Change it and turn on two-step verification.

slides.title: Choose a safer next step
slides.body: Select a scenario to reveal a response. Explain what evidence would change your decision.
cards: An unknown USB drive is on the desk
Do not connect it, even to find the owner. Give it to the instructor or lab staff.
A calculator site asks for camera access
Deny it unless the task has a clear, trusted need.
A message says you must pay a fee to keep your VA benefits
Do not pay or use its link. VA says it never charges fees to apply for benefits and never threatens you by email. Call a number from VA.gov or your benefit letter.
Your home computer still runs Windows 10
Free security updates ended October 2025. Enroll in Extended Security Updates (until October 2027) or move to a supported device, then check Windows Update.

slides.title: Encryption protects readable data
slides.body: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Device encryption (BitLocker in Windows, FileVault on a Mac) protects a lost computer that is turned off. A signed-in computer is open to anyone at the keyboard, so press Windows logo key and L when you step away.

slides.title: Passwords protect different actions
slides.body: In Word, Encrypt with Password sets a password to open and encrypts the file. Always Open Read-Only and Restrict Editing only limit changes; anyone can still read the text. Word cannot recover a lost password, so keep it somewhere safe, away from the file.

slides.title: Unknown devices can carry risk
slides.body: An unknown USB drive can carry malware: software made to harm a computer or steal information. Do not plug it in to find its owner; give it to lab staff. Keep Windows and your browser updated, because updates fix known security holes.

slides.title: Control camera and microphone access
slides.body: Allow the camera or microphone only when the task needs it and you trust the site. A permission can stay on after a call, so review it in your browser’s site permissions. Block requests unrelated to what you are doing.

slides.title: Watch: pause, verify, protect
slides.body: Follow the worked examples, pause for practice, and choose a chapter to replay a skill. Connect the task to a household or community situation you know.

slides.title: Practice the whole routine
slides.body: Skills challenge: on your own, show five skills from this course. Refine a search, build a structured paragraph, total four costs, bring back deleted text and write useful feedback. Leave your work on screen for your instructor.

slides.title: Knowledge check: encryption
slides.body: What is encryption designed to do?
options: Shrink a file so it takes less space
Keep data unreadable without the key
Let people read a file but not change it
slides.why: Encryption keeps data unreadable without the key. Shrinking a file is compression, and read-only only limits changes. Encryption also does not prove a sender or website is honest.

slides.title: Knowledge check: camera access
slides.body: After a video visit, your browser still lets the clinic’s website use your camera and microphone. What is a sensible next step?
options: Leave it; permissions end when the call ends
Review the permission and block it if not needed
Block the camera for every website on this computer
slides.why: A site permission can stay on after the call. Review it in your browser’s site permissions and block it if you no longer need it. Blocking every site would also stop the video visits you need.

slides.title: Take the post-test
slides.body: Type your name first, then answer on your own. When you finish, print page 1 of your results or save it as a PDF, and give your score out of 20 to your instructor.

slides.title: Read your results as a learning plan
slides.body: Look at domain scores and missed questions. Choose one task to practice next. These classroom checks do not award IC3 certification.

Press Windows logo key and + to zoom in. Press Windows logo key and Esc to close Magnifier.
